body:
Mulshankar Harinand Mulani

Mulshankar Mulani was a prominent playwright of professional Gujarati theatre. His plays contributed to the popularity and artistic development of the Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali.

His dramatic repertoire included romantic, historical, mythological and social subjects. He wrote for performing companies, making the actual presentation of his plays before audiences central to his work.

Saubhagya Sundari (1901)

Saubhagya Sundari is one of the best-known plays associated with Mulani. It was performed by the Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali on 19 October 1901.

The original script was written by Nathuram Sundarji Shukla. Mulani extensively rewrote its plot, dialogue and characters for the theatrical company. The successful stage version is therefore commonly credited to Mulani.

The celebrated actor Jayshankar Bhojak played the female character Sundari. His performance became so famous that he acquired the popular name Jayshankar Sundari.

This illustrates the historical practice of male actors portraying female characters in professional Gujarati theatre.

Other works of Mulani

  • Rajbeej
  • Ajabkumari
  • Nandbatrisi
  • Krishnacharitra
  • Devkanya

Another major personality of the Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali was Bapulal Nayak, who contributed as an actor, director and company proprietor. He and Jayshankar Sundari were particularly important figures in the company's performing tradition.

Prabhulal Dayaram Dwivedi

Prabhulal Dwivedi (1892–1962), associated with Virpur in Saurashtra, was an influential playwright and songwriter of the old Gujarati stage.

His works included historical dramas, mythological subjects and plays concerning contemporary social problems. He became particularly associated with Laxmikant Natak Samaj and Deshi Natak Samaj.

Malavpati Munj (1924)

Malavpati Munj, also known as Malavpati, is a historical play based on the story of the Paramara ruler Munja of Malwa. Its dramatic treatment was influenced by K. M. Munshi's historical novel Prithivivallabh (1921).

Prabhulal Dwivedi wrote the play for Laxmikant Natak Samaj, which staged it in 1924. It also entered the repertoire of other companies.

The actor and singer Master Ashraf Khan became famous for portraying Munj. The production was especially remembered for its historical subject, memorable dialogue and popular stage songs.

Vadilona Vanke (1938)

Vadilona Vanke, meaning through the fault of elders, is an important social play written by Prabhulal Dwivedi. It was first performed by Deshi Natak Samaj at Bhangwadi Theatre on 2 April 1938.

The play is distinguished from his historical dramas by its focus on family and social relationships. Its female-centred narrative and memorable songs contributed to its immense popularity.

Major works of Prabhulal Dwivedi

PlayYearCompany association
Arunodaya1921Laxmikant Natak Samaj
Malavpati Munj1924Laxmikant Natak Samaj
Prithviraj1925Laxmikant Natak Samaj
Sirajuddaula1926Laxmikant Natak Samaj
Vadilona Vanke1938Deshi Natak Samaj
Same Paar1947Deshi Natak Samaj

Other works associated with Prabhulal include Sansarsagar, Ek Abala, Shankaracharya and Vidyavaridhi Bharavi.

Playwright and performer are different associations

Mulshankar Mulani is associated with the successful dramatic version of Saubhagya Sundari, while Jayshankar Sundari is remembered for acting in it. Prabhulal Dwivedi wrote Malavpati Munj, while Master Ashraf Khan became famous for portraying Munj.

Prelims focus

  • Mulshankar Mulani: Saubhagya Sundari, Ajabkumari and Rajbeej.
  • 1901: Saubhagya Sundari, Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali.
  • Jayshankar Bhojak earned the name Sundari through his stage role.
  • 1924: Malavpati Munj, Prabhulal Dwivedi and Master Ashraf Khan.
  • 1938: Vadilona Vanke, Deshi Natak Samaj.
  • Trap: K. M. Munshi wrote Prithivivallabh; Prabhulal Dwivedi wrote the related play Malavpati Munj.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, Mulshankar Harinand Mulani, Saubhagya Sundari, Bapulal Nayak, Prabhulal Dwivedi, Malavpati Munj, Prithivivallabh, Vadilona Vanke, Laxmikant Natak Samaj and Deshi Natak Samaj. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Mulshankar Mulani, Prabhulal Dwivedi and the Famous Plays of the Old Stage

body:
Music in the old Gujarati theatre

Music occupied a central place in professional Gujarati theatre during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Songs were incorporated into dramatic scenes to express emotions, reveal a character's feelings and reinforce the subject of a play.

Many theatrical productions combined spoken dialogue with songs. Consequently, actors who could also sing became particularly important to the old stage.

Gujarati theatre songs drew upon familiar musical and poetic traditions, including devotional compositions, romantic songs and Garba. Their popularity extended beyond theatre halls, and many songs survived in public memory even when the original plays ceased to be regularly performed.

Important stage songs and their plays

Several Gujarati stage songs are commonly identified by their opening words. Their original dramatic associations are important because later recordings and independent musical performances may make their theatrical origins less apparent.

Stage songAssociated play
Ek Sarkha Divas Sukhna Koi Na Jata NathiMalavpati Munj
Hrudayna Shuddha PremineMalavpati Munj
Mitha Lagya Te Mane Aajna UjagaraVadilona Vanke
Sahyabo Maro Gulabno ChhodHansakumari
Jhat Jao Chandanhar LavoVallabhipati
Sambhale Re Balpanna SambharanaShalivahan
Tame Jojo Na Vayda VitavjoArunodaya
Rasila Premina HaiyaShalivahan

Important songwriters and performers

Prabhulal Dwivedi

Prabhulal Dwivedi contributed both dramatic scripts and songs to Gujarati professional theatre. His play Malavpati Munj contained several celebrated songs. Master Ashraf Khan's singing helped make them widely popular.

The two celebrated Malavpati songs, Ek Sarkha Divas Sukhna and Hrudayna Shuddha Premine, are closely associated with Prabhulal. Gujarati Vishwakosh also records Raghunath Brahmbhatt's collaborative contribution to these compositions. Their association with Malavpati Munj is clear, even where accounts differ in how they attribute individual lyrics.

Prabhulal's Vadilona Vanke contained the famous song Mitha Lagya Te Mane Aajna Ujagara. It was popularised on the stage by the actress and singer Motibai.

Raghunath Brahmbhatt

Raghunath Brahmbhatt was a playwright and important writer of Gujarati stage songs. Among his well-known compositions are Sahyabo Maro Gulabno Chhod, associated with Hansakumari, and Rasila Premina Haiya, associated with Shalivahan.

He also wrote dramatic works including Suryakumari, Chhatravijay and Ushakumari. His contribution demonstrates that a stage songwriter could write songs both for personal dramatic works and for plays written by other playwrights.

Garba in professional theatre

Dahyabhai Dholashaji Zaveri helped popularise Garba through professional theatre. The productions of Ashrumati (1895) and Veenaveli (1899) by Deshi Natak Samaj incorporated Garba into their dramatic presentation.

Gujarati stage music therefore developed through both newly written theatrical songs and the adaptation of existing regional musical traditions.

Recognise four different artistic roles

The playwright writes the dramatic work, the lyricist writes the song, the composer creates its musical setting, and the singer or actor performs it. These roles may be performed by the same person, but they are not necessarily identical.

Prelims focus

  • Ek Sarkha Divas Sukhna and Hrudayna Shuddha Premine: Malavpati Munj.
  • Mitha Lagya Te Mane Aajna Ujagara: Vadilona Vanke.
  • Sahyabo Maro Gulabno Chhod: Hansakumari; Raghunath Brahmbhatt.
  • Sambhale Re Balpanna Sambharana: Shalivahan.
  • Tame Jojo Na Vayda Vitavjo: Arunodaya.
  • Trap: The performer who popularised a stage song is not necessarily its lyricist.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarat: Fine Arts to Mass Media, theatre and stage songs section; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Malavpati Munj, Prithivivallabh, Raghunath Brahmbhatt and Deshi Natak Samaj; Gujaratilexicon, Songs of the Old Gujarati Theatre; Opinion Magazine, Mitha Lagya Te Mane Aajna Ujagara, reproduced from Mumbai Samachar, 19 September 2019. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Gujarati Rangbhumi Songs and Their Associated Plays

body:
The transition towards modern theatre

During the first half of the 20th century, Gujarati theatre began to expand beyond the established system of professional travelling companies. Educated writers, students, cultural organisations and amateur theatre groups became increasingly involved in writing and presenting plays.

The older commercial stage had established a large audience for drama. However, a new generation of playwrights sought to explore contemporary social life, realistic characters, literary subjects and new dramatic forms.

This development did not completely replace professional theatre. Amateur, literary and commercial theatre continued to exist alongside one another.

Chandravadan Chimanlal Mehta

Chandravadan Mehta (1901–1991), also known as C. C. Mehta, was born in Surat and had an important association with Vadodara. He is regarded as a pioneer of modern Gujarati theatre.

His contribution extended beyond writing plays. He worked as an actor, director and promoter of theatrical education and amateur dramatic activity.

He encouraged the presentation of plays as serious artistic and literary works rather than treating them exclusively as commercial entertainment.

Aag Gadi (1934)

Aag Gadi, also written as Agagadi, is Chandravadan Mehta's landmark play. Its subject is the life of railway workers under British rule.

The central narrative concerns Badharji, a railway fireman who suffers under the discriminatory and oppressive behaviour of a British engine driver. The play uses the everyday world of railway workers to portray social inequality and human suffering.

Instead of relying primarily on legendary rulers or mythological stories, the play presents ordinary working people and a recognisable contemporary social environment. This made it an important work in the movement towards realistic Gujarati drama.

The work is dated 1934. Gujarat College students participated in an Ahmedabad production in 1935, and Chandravadan Mehta presented it at New Era School in Bombay in 1936.

He received the Ranjitram Suvarna Chandrak in 1936 for Aag Gadi.

Other important plays

PlayYear
Akho1927
Narmad1937
Sita1943
Dhara Gurjari1944
Panjarapol1947

These works illustrate the variety of his dramatic interests. He drew upon Gujarati literary personalities, social subjects, mythology and cultural identity.

Amateur theatre and cultural institutions

The amateur theatre movement provided opportunities for actors and playwrights outside the traditional company system. Colleges, cultural associations and literary institutions helped organise performances and develop new audiences.

Important organisations associated with this development included:

  • Natmandal: Ahmedabad; associated with Gujarat Vidyasabha.
  • Rangmandal: Ahmedabad.
  • Indian National Theatre: Bombay.
  • Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan's Kalakendra: Bombay.
  • Nadiad Kala Mandir: Nadiad.

Some institutions later contributed significantly to professional and commercial theatre as well. The distinction between amateur and professional theatre describes the organisation and purpose of theatrical activity rather than an absolute division between particular artists.

Old and modern theatre

Old professional theatre companies sustained Gujarati drama through repeated public performances and popular musical productions. Modern theatre expanded this tradition through realistic writing, educational institutions, amateur groups and literary experimentation.

Neither period was restricted to a single type of subject. The old stage also presented social problems, and modern theatre continued to use mythology, history, music and folk traditions.

Prelims focus

  • Chandravadan Mehta: pioneer of modern Gujarati theatre.
  • Aag Gadi (1934): Chandravadan Mehta.
  • Aag Gadi portrays railway workers and colonial social inequality.
  • 1936: Ranjitram Suvarna Chandrak for Aag Gadi.
  • Natmandal and Rangmandal: Ahmedabad.
  • Trap: Ranchhodbhai Dave is associated with the foundations of Gujarati drama; Chandravadan Mehta is particularly associated with its modern development.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, Chandravadan Chimanlal Mehta and Aag Gadi; D. G. Vyas, Gujarati Drama, Indian Drama, Publications Division, Government of India, November 1956, particularly p. 60. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Chandravadan Mehta and the Rise of Modern Gujarati Theatre

body:
Folk traditions in modern Gujarati theatre

Modern Gujarati theatre developed not only through Western influence and realistic drama but also through a renewed interest in indigenous theatrical traditions.

Bhavai offered playwrights and directors a rich source of regional stories, music, humour and social expression. Modern productions adapted these elements into written plays and presented them to urban as well as rural audiences.

Natmandal and Gujarat Vidyasabha

Natmandal emerged as an important theatre institution in Ahmedabad under the auspices of Gujarat Vidyasabha, formerly known as the Gujarat Vernacular Society.

It helped bring literary drama and traditional Gujarati theatre into contact with one another. Its productions benefited from the experience of established artists such as Jayshankar Sundari and Pransukh Nayak, as well as performers belonging to a newer generation.

The successful 1953 production of Dalpatram's Mithyabhiman demonstrated how a 19th-century literary play could be revived through modern theatrical organisation.

Mena Gurjari

Mena Gurjari, also written as Mena Gujari or Menan Gurjari, is an important Gujarati dramatic work by Rasiklal Chhotalal Parikh.

Its subject was derived from a traditional Gujarati Garba concerning Mena, a woman of the Gurjar community. The narrative celebrates courage, dignity and self-respect.

The work first appeared in the literary periodical Prasthan in 1930. It subsequently achieved widespread recognition through Natmandal's musical theatrical productions during the 1950s.

Jayshankar Sundari was associated with the direction of the famous production, while Dina Pathak, also known earlier as Dina Gandhi, became celebrated for performing the title role.

The play brought together Gujarati folk narrative, music, dance and dramatic performance. It illustrates how a story from regional oral tradition could become a major work of organised modern theatre.

The principal author of Mena Gurjari was Rasiklal Parikh. Dina Pathak was its celebrated performer, and Natmandal was the institution associated with its famous theatrical presentation.

Jasma Odan

Jasma Odan, also written as Jasma Odhan, is based on a traditional Gujarati folk legend that also forms part of the Bhavai repertoire.

The legend concerns Jasma, a woman of the Oad community, and her determination to protect her dignity and fidelity. It is popularly associated with Siddharaj Jaysinh and the Sahasralinga Talav tradition of Patan.

The traditional narrative predates its modern theatrical adaptation. Shanta Gandhi drew upon this folk material and the Bhavai form to develop a significant modern production.

Her production of Jasma Odan at the National School of Drama in New Delhi in 1968 became an important example of the use of indigenous folk theatre in modern Indian drama.

Distinguishing the two folk-based plays

FeatureMena GurjariJasma Odan
Folk sourceTraditional Garba narrativeGujarati folk legend and Bhavai vesha
Modern creative associationRasiklal ParikhShanta Gandhi
Prominent institutional associationNatmandal, AhmedabadNational School of Drama, New Delhi
Major stage period1950s1968 landmark production

Dina Pathak and Shanta Gandhi were sisters, both of whom made important contributions to theatre. Their artistic associations should nevertheless be distinguished: Dina Pathak is particularly remembered for her performance in Mena Gurjari, while Shanta Gandhi is closely associated with the modern presentation of Jasma Odan.

Prelims focus

  • Mena Gurjari: Rasiklal Parikh.
  • Mena Gurjari: traditional Garba narrative and Natmandal.
  • Dina Pathak: celebrated performer of Mena.
  • Jasma Odan: Gujarati folk legend and Bhavai tradition.
  • Shanta Gandhi: modern Jasma Odan production, 1968.
  • Trap: Shanta Gandhi adapted an existing folk narrative; she did not originate the traditional legend of Jasma.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, Mena Gurjari, Mithyabhiman and Gujarat: Fine Arts to Mass Media; Times of India, Mena Gurjari Staged in Ahmedabad After 62 Years, 28 March 2014; Scroll, When Struggling to Define Modern Theatre, a Young India Found Inspiration in Its Folk Past, section on Jasma Odan; Sahapedia, A Brief Introduction to Bhavai. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
